        05 / THE IDEA BEHIND IT

        Tri-Anchor + Hop

        A custom remaining-distance estimate for A*. Three reference cities and a minimum road count provide four lower bounds. We keep the strongest one.

        UCS: f(n) = g(n)
        A*: f(n) = g(n) + h(n)

        g(n) is the cost of the best route found so far from the start to city n. h(n) estimates the remaining cost from n to the selected goal. A* selects the frontier city with the lowest f(n).

        THE COMBINED HEURISTIC

        Four bounds.
        One remaining estimate.

        h(n, t) = max(
        bArad, bNeamt, bEforie, 70 × H(n, t)
        )

        t is the selected goal. H(n, t) is the fewest roads needed to reach it. Each b is a landmark distance bound, explained below. All four bounds are in kilometres.

        This live calculation follows the city selected in the search playback.

        01 / THREE ANCHORS

        Distances from three reference cities

        “Tri” means three. Our anchors are Arad, Neamt, and Eforie, spread across the west, northeast, and southeast of the map. They give different reference points. This is a fixed design choice, not a claim that these are the best possible landmarks.

        At startup, Dijkstra’s algorithm calculates the shortest road distance from each anchor to every city. Call that distance D(L, x), where L is an anchor and x is a city. For each anchor, calculate:

        bL(n, t) = |D(L, n) − D(L, t)|

        The absolute difference tells us how far apart n and t must be, at minimum. If they are 140 km and 418 km from the same anchor, they must be at least 278 km apart by road. The route does not have to pass through that anchor.

        02 / THE HOP BOUND

        Count the roads still needed

        A hop means crossing one road to a neighboring city. A breadth-first search from the goal counts the fewest hops from every city, temporarily ignoring the different road lengths.

        hop bound = H(n, t) × 70 km

        The shortest road in this map is Lugoj–Mehadia, 70 km. If every possible route needs at least two roads, and every road is at least 70 km, the remaining journey must cost at least 140 km. The route with the fewest roads may differ from the route with the lowest total distance.

        03 / WHY MAXIMUM?

        Keep the strongest safe estimate

        Each bound describes the same remaining journey. If the four bounds are 43, 43, 43, and 140 km, we know the journey must be at least 140 km. Taking the maximum retains the most useful information without exceeding the true shortest distance.

        Adding the bounds could count the same distance multiple times and overestimate. “Tri-Anchor + Hop” names the combination of techniques. Within h, we use max. The addition happens in A* priority: f = g + h.

        04 / WORKED EXAMPLES

        How the numbers guide A*

        Arad to Bucharest, considering Sibiu: the route found to Sibiu costs g = 140 km. The remaining estimate uses Sibiu and Bucharest:

        Bounds at Sibiu with Bucharest as the goal
        ComponentCalculationBound
        Arad anchor|140 − 418|278 km
        Neamt anchor|684 − 406|278 km
        Eforie anchor|547 − 269|278 km
        Hop count2 × 70140 km

        h(Sibiu) = max(278, 278, 278, 140) = 278 km
        f(Sibiu) = 140 + 278 = 418 km

        The two-hop route is through Fagaras. The cheapest remaining route uses three roads through Rimnicu Vilcea and Pitesti. The estimate happens to be exact here because Arad is a landmark on the optimal route.

        Where Hop helps: Zerind to Timisoara. All three landmark bounds are 43 km. The minimum is two hops, giving 140 km. The combination therefore raises h from 43 to 140 km, still below the actual shortest distance of 193 km.

        h comes from the bounds for the current city and goal. It is not generally “the initial estimate minus g.” Priority can change between cities. At the goal h = 0, so f = g.

        05 / THE CODE

        Preparation, then priority

        1. Once per map: build the three landmark distance tables with Dijkstra.
        2. For the chosen goal: run BFS to count hops and combine the four bounds for every city. Any of the 20 cities can be the goal.
        3. During A*: update g using the real road costs and select the lowest g + h. The prepared h for a city stays fixed for that goal and map.
        View the heuristic function used by this app
        export function heuristicFor(goal){
 validateCity(goal);
 const hops=new Int16Array(cities.length).fill(-1);hops[goal]=0;const q=[goal];
 for(let i=0;i<q.length;i++)for(const e of graph[q[i]])if(hops[e.id]===-1){hops[e.id]=hops[q[i]]+1;q.push(e.id);}
 return Float64Array.from(cities,(_,n)=>Math.max(minimumEdge*hops[n],...landmarkTables.map(d=>Math.abs(d[n]-d[goal]))));
}

        minimumEdge is the minimum road cost, 70 here. landmarkTables contains the three Dijkstra distance tables. q is the BFS queue. Math.abs calculates each anchor bound and Math.max selects the largest.

        06 / CORRECTNESS AND TRADEOFFS

        Useful guidance has a cost

        Admissible means h never exceeds the true shortest remaining distance. Consistent means h(u) ≤ road cost(u, v) + h(v) across every road. Both hold for our bounds on this undirected map, and h is zero at the goal. A* therefore preserves the optimal path cost when it selects the goal from the frontier.

        Why these properties hold

        The triangle inequality gives |D(L, u) − D(L, t)| ≤ D(u, t). Across a road of cost w, a landmark bound changes by at most w. The hop counts satisfy H(u, t) ≤ 1 + H(v, t). Multiplying by 70 preserves consistency because every road costs at least 70. Taking the maximum preserves both admissibility and consistency.

        Guidance can reduce city expansions, but preparing and storing the bounds adds work. A* is not guaranteed to run faster, especially on a 20-city map. Compare measured search time, preparation time, expansions, and estimated storage separately. When roads change, recompute the bounds.

        What is custom? The name, fixed three-anchor choice, and combination with the hop bound describe this project’s heuristic. A* and landmark bounds are established ideas. We do not claim a new search algorithm. The core landmark technique appears in Goldberg and Harrelson’s work on A*, landmarks, and the triangle inequality.

        The repository tests compare all 400 ordered start–goal pairs against an independent shortest-path calculation and check the heuristic’s bounds and consistency. For a fair demonstration, include a route such as Lugoj to Vaslui, where neither endpoint is a landmark.

        How the comparison is measured

        Path cost: the sum of road distances. Expanded nodes: cities whose outgoing roads were examined; selecting the goal does not count as an expansion. Ties use alphabetical city order for both algorithms.

        Runtime: median per-search duration across 15 batches of 100 runs, after 100 warm-up runs per algorithm. Execution order alternates by batch. Animation and trace recording are excluded. A* goal preparation and one-time landmark preparation are reported separately. These tiny searches are sensitive to timer precision, browser activity, and hardware; A* may not be faster.

        Memory model: typed arrays for costs (160 B), parents (40 B), and explored flags (20 B), plus 8 B per peak frontier entry. A* additionally retains 480 B of landmark distances and 160 B of goal heuristic values. These figures exclude JavaScript object overhead, temporary preprocessing storage, map data, and visualization history. Peak stored cities and frontier size are also reported. This is a reproducible storage estimate, not a measurement of process RAM.
